items.title: Grids & spacing
items.description: Why some screens feel off — and how a grid and spacing scale fix it.

metadata.practise: Fix a messy screen with 3 text styles (Stage 02 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Grids and spacing in UI design: a beginner's guide
metadata.seoDescription: Why do some screens feel off? Usually it's the gaps. Learn grids, gutters, margins and a simple spacing scale you can reuse everywhere.

quiz.question: What is a gutter?
quiz.why: Gutters are the gaps between columns that stop content from touching.

quiz.question: Why use a spacing scale?
options: Fewer decisions and more consistent layouts
quiz.why: Choosing from a few set values saves time and makes everything feel consistent.

quiz.question: Which statement about the 8-point scale is accurate?
options: It's a popular habit that works well, not a law
quiz.why: It's a convention. Use it because it helps, not because someone says you must.

quiz.question: White space is...
options: What lets important things stand out
quiz.why: Breathing room guides attention and makes screens feel calmer.

items.title: Typography basics
items.description: Most of an interface is words. Make them easy to read.

metadata.practise: Fix a messy screen with 3 text styles (Stage 02 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Typography basics for UI designers: size, weight and readability
metadata.seoDescription: Most of an interface is words. Learn the basics of type: typefaces, size, line height, line length and a tiny type scale you can reuse.

quiz.question: What is line height?
options: The space from one line of text to the next
quiz.why: Line height controls how much room lines have, which strongly affects readability.

quiz.question: How many typefaces should a beginner start with?
quiz.why: One typeface in several weights is enough for most screens. Fewer choices means more consistency.

quiz.question: Why are very long lines of text a problem?
options: It's harder for eyes to track back to the next line
quiz.why: Readers lose their place on very long lines, so comfort drops.

quiz.question: What's the first job of typography?
quiz.why: If people can't read it comfortably, nothing else about it matters.

items.title: Alignment & proximity
items.description: Put related things close together and line things up. That's most of the fix.

metadata.practise: Fix a messy screen with 3 text styles (Stage 02 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Alignment and proximity in design: fix messy layouts fast
metadata.seoDescription: Two ideas fix most messy screens: put related things close together, and line things up. Learn proximity, alignment and grouping without clutter.

quiz.question: What does proximity say?
options: Things that are close together look like they belong together
quiz.why: Distance tells the eye what's related, even before it reads anything.

quiz.question: Where should a form label sit?
options: Closer to its own field than to the field above
At the bottom of the page
quiz.why: Proximity tells people which label belongs to which field.

quiz.question: Why are left-aligned paragraphs easier to read in English?
options: The eye returns to the same starting edge on each line
quiz.why: A shared starting edge makes it easier to find the next line.

quiz.question: What should you try before adding borders to group things?
quiz.why: Space groups things quietly without adding visual noise.

items.title: Visual hierarchy
items.description: Decide what people see first, second and third.

metadata.practise: Fix a messy screen with 3 text styles (Stage 02 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Visual hierarchy in UI design: what people see first
metadata.seoDescription: Visual hierarchy decides what people notice first, second and third. Learn the three volume knobs, the squint test and how to find your one main thing.

quiz.question: What does visual hierarchy do?
options: Shows people what to look at first, second and third
quiz.why: Hierarchy is the order of attention, so people don't have to guess.

quiz.question: If you make everything bold, what happens?
quiz.why: Emphasis only works when it's rare. When everything shouts, nothing does.

quiz.question: What's the squint test for?
options: Seeing what stands out when details blur
quiz.why: Blur strips away the details so you can see the real order of attention.

quiz.question: Ideally, how many primary actions should one screen have?
quiz.why: One clear main action makes the next step obvious.

items.title: Color & contrast
items.description: Use color with restraint and keep every pair readable.

metadata.youllNeed: A free Figma account and a contrast checker (free online tools or a Figma plugin).
metadata.practise: Fix a messy screen with 3 text styles (Stage 02 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Color and contrast in UI design: a beginner's guide
metadata.seoDescription: Give every color a job, keep your palette small, and make text readable for everyone. Learn contrast ratios, status colors and why color alone isn't enough.

quiz.question: At the AA level, what's the minimum contrast ratio for normal text?
quiz.why: WCAG's AA level asks for at least 4.5 to 1 for normal-sized text and 3 to 1 for large text.

quiz.question: A form field turns red on error, with no other change. What's the problem?
options: Not everyone can tell color changes apart
quiz.why: Pairing color with an icon and a message means everyone gets the signal.

quiz.question: Most of a screen should be...
quiz.why: A calm neutral base lets the accent do its job.

quiz.question: What should you do before falling in love with a color combination?
quiz.why: It's easier to adjust early than to redesign after everything is built.

items.title: Responsive layout
items.description: Design one system that adapts from phone to desktop.

metadata.upNextLabel: Stage 03, Who are you designing for?
metadata.practise: Fix a messy screen with 3 text styles (Stage 02 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Responsive layout: design that fits every screen
metadata.seoDescription: Learn what responsive layout means, why mobile-first works, and how fluid layouts and breakpoints help your design fit phones, tablets and desktops.

quiz.question: What does "mobile first" mean?
options: Designing the small screen first, then expanding
quiz.why: Starting small forces you to prioritize, then you add as space grows.

quiz.question: What is a breakpoint?
options: A screen width where the layout changes
quiz.why: Breakpoints mark where the layout needs to switch to look good.

quiz.question: Why set a maximum width on a desktop layout?
options: So text lines don't become too long to read comfortably
quiz.why: Very long lines are tiring to read, even on a big screen.

quiz.question: What should decide where a breakpoint goes?
options: Where your content starts looking bad
quiz.why: Common breakpoints are conventions. Your content is the real guide.
